items.title: Faithful and Complete LLM-Assisted Automated Construction of Hierarchical Hardware Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: The research presents an automated pipeline using Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs from hardware datasheets. This process involves chunk-based property extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement to handle the fragmented and heterogeneous information in datasheets. The framework utilizes LLMs for extraction and reasoning while ensuring source provenance and traceable execution for reliable results. Evaluation showed the framework achieved 98.8% property faithfulness, significantly outperforming a one-shot baseline of 76.1%. These improvements yield more comprehensive and reliable engineering information for hardware design and verification.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Faithful and Complete LLM-Assisted Automated Construction of Hierarchical Hardware Knowledge Graphs" details an automated pipeline using Large Language Models to construct hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs from hardware datasheets, achieving 98.8 percent property faithfulness in evaluation. The research describes an automated process involving chunk-based property extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement to manage the fragmented and heterogeneous data found in datasheets. This framework employs LLMs for both extraction and reasoning, incorporating mechanisms to ensure source provenance and traceable execution for result reliability. Evaluation demonstrated that this methodology significantly improved accuracy compared to a one-shot baseline of 76.1 percent, resulting in more comprehensive engineering information for hardware design and verification. This work indicates a significant step toward automating the reliable synthesis of complex technical knowledge from raw engineering documents.

items.title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
items.summary: Data-centric scaling of RLVR often results in a "zero-advantage trap" where large datasets offer little useful learning signal. To create effective synthetic data, problems must be calibrated so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one solution is reachable within the training budget. MagicBeanStalk introduces a recursive data-synthesis algorithm to grow seed problems into new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems. This method improved performance on math benchmarks and finance tasks by synthesizing problems that require necessary reasoning. The approach successfully generated verifiable problems to escape the limitations of simply pooling large corpora.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis" details a method for generating useful training data in reinforcement learning environments. This research introduces a recursive data-synthesis algorithm designed to overcome the zero-advantage trap encountered when scaling reinforcement learning with large datasets. The methodology involves calibrating problems so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one solution remains reachable within the training budget to ensure meaningful learning signals. The MagicBeanStalk approach grows seed problems into new training problems through recursive synthesis, effectively generating verifiable problems that require necessary reasoning. This process improved performance on mathematics benchmarks and finance tasks by synthesizing problems that demand specific reasoning capabilities, moving beyond simple data pooling. This work indicates a pathway toward more efficient and higher-quality data-centric scaling in reinforcement learning systems.

items.title: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
items.summary: EvoSyn is a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework designed for agentic data synthesis in closed-loop learning. It addresses the gap where observed weaknesses do not directly inform future synthesis, by organizing synthesis around a revisable state of interaction factors. A multi-agent system translates learner feedback into synthesis revisions, guided by a Designer allocating synthesis directions and a Planner grounding them into executable experience. This process allows for adaptation toward weak regions and the expansion of the synthesis space to incorporate newly discovered factors. Experiments demonstrated that EvoSyn improved task success and generated higher-quality, broader synthetic experience.

items.title: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
items.summary: The method aligns two unimodal encoders using only a small number of paired data points through distilled optimal transport. It achieves this by representing all modalities based on their similarity to these anchors, placing them in a common coordinate system. A single entropic optimal transport problem solves the matching between the two point clouds, counteracting hubness in nearest-neighbor matching. The resulting plan is distilled into lightweight encoders, making the correspondence inductive. This approach outperforms existing methods in image-text and molecule-text alignment tasks.

items.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.summary: SpireBench evaluates the long-horizon strategic play of agentic models using the commercial deck-builder game Slay the Spire. The benchmark tests how models make sequential decisions over extended gameplay, assessing stored knowledge, reasoning, and luck management. Frontier LLMs perform better than heuristic baselines and match average human performance in initial phases, but performance degrades as the run lengthens. The study indicates that performance differences stem from how agents manage risk across the entire run, rather than simple memory retention. SpireBench provides a comprehensive, unsaturated benchmark with tools to pinpoint where and why agents make strategic errors.

The study assessed how models manage sequential decisions over extended gameplay, focusing on stored knowledge, reasoning, and luck management. The methodology involved applying agentic models to the game, measuring performance across lengthy strategic runs. Frontier Large Language Models demonstrated superior performance compared to heuristic baselines and achieved performance levels comparable to average human play in the initial stages of the game. However, performance experienced a degradation as the game runs extended, suggesting that performance differences are rooted in the agents' management of risk throughout the entire sequence rather than just simple memory retention. SpireBench offers a comprehensive benchmark to identify specific points of strategic error in agentic systems. This research indicates a need for evaluation metrics that capture long-term risk management in artificial intelligence agents.

items.title: CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents
items.summary: The CLEAT framework learns value-guided clarification to assist interactive agents in handling incomplete information. It co-trains a clarification-value controller and a task policy using shared interaction outcomes. Residual query value measures the task utility gained by asking a question instead of proceeding immediately. Paired rollouts from interaction history train the controller to predict clarification value and the policy to select useful questions. This method improves agent performance, achieving significant gains on evaluation benchmarks.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents" details a framework designed to help interactive agents manage incomplete information effectively. The method co-trains a clarification-value controller and a task policy by sharing interaction outcomes to learn value-guided clarification. Residual query value measures the utility gained from asking a question versus immediate action, and paired rollouts from interaction history train the controller to predict clarification value and the policy to select beneficial questions. This process results in improved agent performance demonstrating significant gains on relevant evaluation benchmarks. The development signals a step toward more robust and contextually aware interactive agents capable of navigating ambiguity in complex environments.

items.title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
items.summary: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm utilizing large language models to guide the exploration of executable control policies. It uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to inform new proposals, edits, and remixes of existing solutions. Performance was assessed across six Gymnasium control tasks, with results showing increased candidate-score medians over generations. Gains were observed in some tasks, such as in CartPole-v1, where the selected winner reached the score ceiling quickly. The method demonstrated the improvement of program search and the transfer of gains to new episodes in certain tasks.

items.title: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
items.summary: A computational study compared Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and randomized-restart list scheduling for Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) workflows under an equal budget. MCTS performed 2.88% worse than the restarts, although the deficit was not due to budget starvation. Restarts showed self-improvement on the separate exploration pool, whereas MCTS gains were minimal. The performance difference was workflow-dependent, with restarts outperforming MCTS on sparse irregular workflows. Using textbook UCT instead of the main MCTS rule reduced the deficit significantly.

The study found that while Monte Carlo Tree Search performed slightly worse than the randomized-restart method, the performance difference was not attributable to budget starvation. The methodology involved comparing these two scheduling algorithms on DAG workflows, observing that randomized restarts exhibited self-improvement on the separate exploration pool, whereas Monte Carlo Tree Search demonstrated minimal gains. items.title: Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents
items.summary: Verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning often use binary feedback, which is insufficient for fine-grained debugging quality assessment in software engineering agents. Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR) is introduced as a method to allow policies to judge their own trajectories to improve performance. BSR reuses the policy to compare observable debugging behaviors across trajectories from the same task and verifier outcome. It aggregates these pairwise preferences into task-local scores, creating auxiliary rewards that offer contrast without ignoring the initial pass/fail ordering. Experiments on SWE-bench demonstrate that this approach consistently improves performance for Qwen3 models.
items.audio_script: From arXiv - cs.AI, "Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents" details a method for improving software engineering agent performance by introducing behavioral self-rewarding mechanisms. This research introduces Behavioral Self-Rewarding as a technique to move beyond binary feedback in reinforcement learning by enabling policies to evaluate their own trajectories for performance enhancement. The method involves reusing the policy to compare observable debugging behaviors across multiple trajectories for the same task and verifier outcome. This process aggregates pairwise preferences into task-local scores, generating auxiliary rewards that provide contrast without disregarding the initial pass or fail ordering. Experiments conducted on the SWE-bench dataset demonstrated that this approach consistently improved performance for Qwen3 models. This advancement suggests a pathway toward more nuanced and effective self-improvement in autonomous software development systems.

items.title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance
items.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) methods often oversimplify model internals, leading to a misalignment between explanations and the model, known as unfaithfulness. Faithfulness is defined as the degree of approximation between an explanation and the model, and measuring it rigorously is important for trustworthiness. Current faithfulness metrics suffer from significant limitations, making accurate quantification of this faithfulness either infeasible or computationally expensive. This position paper outlines five major shortcomings of existing metrics. It proposes four research directions to improve the reliability of faithfulness quantification.

The position paper outlines five major shortcomings of existing faithfulness metrics, highlighting a misalignment between explanations and the model, termed unfaithfulness, and emphasizing the importance of rigorously measuring faithfulness. The paper discusses how current faithfulness metrics face limitations in accurately quantifying this relationship due to inherent complexities in measuring the approximation between an explanation and the model. It proposes four research directions intended to improve the reliability of faithfulness quantification through new methodologies. This research signals a need for refined metrics to ensure the trustworthiness of explanations used in artificial intelligence systems.
